newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end sharply lower, dollar up.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end sharply lower, dollar up.

text.p: New York precious metals futures ended sharply lower Monday, extending the decline of the past month, after gold bullion fixed in London Monday at its lowest level for more than a year at $379.00 an ounce.

"U.S. dollar strength is depressing precious metal demand, particularly in Japan, while healthy U.S. equity and bond markets are providing no incentive for investors in precious metals either," Smith Barney analyst David Rinehimer said.
"During the recent down-move, the more industrial-based precious metals - silver and palladium - have led the decline, pushing the gold/silver ratio up to an 18 month high."

The U.S. dollar hit a 32 month high against the yen at 111.68 yen Monday, while the spot gold/silver ratio ended Monday at 78.00, not far from its September 20 high at 78.55, and up from a low of l73.71 on August 26.
COMEX December gold ended down $2.30 an ounce at $380.50, after seeing a session low at $380.50, a new three year low for the December contract, while back months in gold saw life-of-contract lows.
In New York bullion trade, spot gold ended quoted $378.20/378.60, after gold fixed at $379.00 in London Monday afternoon, the lowest fix since September 6, 1995.
In New York Friday spot gold closed quoted $380.15/380.65.
COMEX December silver ended down 4.3 cents at $4.877 an ounce, after seeing a session low at $4.860, with some months also seeing life-of-contract lows.
The strength of the dollar could be seen in the latest Japanese import data released Monday, analysts said.

Japan's gold imports in August, at 9.53 tonnes, were down 54.1 percent from the same month last year, while gold imports in the first eight months of 1996 totalled 105.08 tonnes, down from 199.47 tonnes in the same period last year.

Japanese platinum imports of 4.61 tonnes in August were down 15.9 percent from August last year, while platinum imports in the first eight months this year were 46.58 tonnes, down from 47.90 tonnes in the same period last year.
NYMEX October platinum ended down $1.20 an ounce at $385.00, after seeing a fresh life-of-contract low at $383.50, while NYMEX December palladium ended down 25 cents at $119.75.
In other news, over the weekend, G-7 ministers approved an IMF third world debt relief plan, but a decision on IMF gold sales to help finance the plan was delayed indefinitely.

Of more immediate concern though was the amount of silver held by Wilmington Trust in Delaware, which becomes an official despositary from January 1. COMEX will release data on Wilmington's holdings early Tuesday. Analysts estimated Wilmington could be holding up to 100 million ounces of silver which could become deliverable from January 1, 1997.

But COMEX silver stocks have declined by more than eight million ounces in the past two weeks, and stood at 141,735,355 ounces Friday, not far from the 1996 low of 139.1 million seen in April, analysts noted.

However, even though fresh lows were seen in precious metals futures Monday, standard technical indicators on the daily charts suggested the momentum of the decline was slowing, with most contracts near oversold levels, and funds already heavily short, analysts said.

In the CFTC Commitment of Traders report, just published for the week ending September 24, "the most glaring story in commodities right now is the all time net short position of large traders in gold," MCM analyst Peter McTeague said.
In the Large Trader category speculators were short 65,772 contracts and long only 9,958 contracts, the report said.
Commercials or hedgers were long 128,476 lots and short 78,937 lots.
-Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, +1-212-859-1641 email: clive.mckeef@reuters.com
